{{short description|British physicist, professor of physics}}
{{Other people|William Mitchell}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Sir Edgar William John Mitchell''', {{postnominals|country=GBR|CBE|FRS|size=100%}}<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Cowley | first1 = R. A. | author-link = Roger Cowley| doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2004.0013 | doi-access = free| title = Sir Edgar William John Mitchell CBE. 25 September 1925 - 30 October 2002: Elected F.R.S. 1980 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 50 | pages = 171 | year = 2004 | s2cid = 71058475 }}</ref> (September 25, 1925 – October 30, 2002) was a British physicist, professor of [[physics]] at [[University of Reading|Reading]] and [[University of Oxford|Oxford]], and he helped pioneer the field of [[neutron scattering]].<ref name=guardian>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2002/nov/12/guardianobituaries.obituaries |title=Obituary: Sir William Mitchell &#124; Education &#124; The Guardian |access-date=2011-07-27 |location=London |first=Pearce |last=Wright |date=November 12, 2002}}</ref>

Born in [[Kingsbridge]], [[Devon]], [[England]], he studied physics at Sheffield University, which had become an important centre for research in radar and defence communications. In 1946, he took up a research position with [[Metropolitan-Vickers]], leading to a secondment to [[Bristol University]], where Nobel laureate [[Nevill Mott]] was head of the department. After gaining his PhD, he took a position at [[Reading University]] in 1951, becoming professor of physics in 1961, and later dean of science and deputy vice chancellor. In 1978 he was named [[Dr Lee's Professor of Experimental Philosophy]] at [[Oxford University]] and became the head of the [[Clarendon laboratory]].<ref name=guardian/>

He was also a skilled administrator who served in many public capacities. He became chairman of [[Science and Engineering Research Council|SERC]] in 1985, at a time of conflict between the British government and higher education over funding and independence. He was vice-president of the [[European Science Foundation]] from 1989 to 1992 and president of [[CERN]] in 1991.<ref name=guardian/> Mitchell was also a member of the [[Science & Environmental Policy Project|SEPP]] Board of Science Advisors. He won the [[Richard Glazebrook Medal and Prize]] in 1996.
